name: John Stuart Mill
worldviewSummary: Mill combines utilitarianism — actions are right in proportion as they promote happiness — with a strong defence of individual liberty. The only legitimate ground for coercing a person against their will is to prevent harm to others; free discussion and 'experiments in living' are essential to human progress and to the development of individuality.
biography: English philosopher and economist, educated intensively by his father James Mill and influenced by Jeremy Bentham. He worked for the East India Company, served as a Member of Parliament, and collaborated intellectually with Harriet Taylor Mill.

concepts.description: The only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over any member of a civilized community, against their will, is to prevent harm to others; their own good is not a sufficient warrant.
Pleasures differ in quality as well as quantity; it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied.
Society can oppress through prevailing opinion and custom as well as through law, which calls for protection of individual dissent.

positions.statement: Silencing an opinion is wrong even if the opinion is false: if it is true we lose truth, if partly true we lose part of it, and if false we lose the livelier understanding of truth produced by its collision with error.
Human nature is not a machine built to a model but a tree that needs to grow on all sides; conformity and custom stunt the faculties that make human life valuable.
Actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness and wrong as they tend to produce its reverse, happiness meaning pleasure and the absence of pain.
The legal subordination of women to men is wrong in itself and a chief hindrance to human improvement; it should be replaced by perfect equality.
The harm principle is meant to apply to adults in mature societies; Mill excluded children and, controversially, societies he considered 'backward'.

relations.note: In Utilitarianism Mill argues Kant's universalizability test only works through appeal to consequences.
